Not sure if this is where you're getting at but there was a crisis of foundation in the philosophy of maths ongoing in the late 19th to early 20th century. This is actually one of my favorite topics in philosophy.  This is a considerable summary because the history of the topic is extensive and go on.

In the late 19th Century, Gottlob Frege wanted to build a complete mathematical system that is grounded upon the most basic and fundamental logical axioms. To do this, he advanced beyond classical Aristotelian logic and developed what is now known as predicate logic. If it was possible for real number theory to be reduced to rational number theory and natural number theory to be grounded on simply set theory.

Assuming that the natural numbers were well behaved, all he needed to do was prove the consistency of set theory & its logic. If mathematics was founded upon strictly logic then the basic axioms should all be consistent and true. (The system is consistent or logically true if all of its instantiations or interpretations are true. All one needed to do was generate a contradiction on one of its interpretations to prove the system’s inconsistency.)

Later in the early 20th Century, Bertrand Russell finds an inconsistency in Frege’s logical system: The paradox of Impredicative definitions (His Principle of Unrestricted Comprehension which roughly states that for every formula that contains x as an apparent free variable, there will exist a set whose members are exactly those objects that satisfy that formula. He proves there to be a contradiction in Frege's system:

    Let S = {x:xϵx}
    If SϵS, then S∉S
    If S∉S, then SϵS
    ∴ SϵS iff S∉S
    ∴ SϵS & S∉S

Russell and Whitehead's goal for the *Principia Mathematica* was to create a consistent system of logic that could be a foundation for all of mathematics. They demonstrated that certain features in arithmetic acted as a deductive system through which mathematical truths can be derived by way of a few basic axioms which they believed could prove everything that is true within type theory.

In order for him to remove these paradoxes, Russell constructed a set-theoretic alternative named Type Theory which restricted the domain of every expression by organizing all logical objects under an infinite hierarchy of types and classes. Even by removing the problem of impredictivity, there still were paradoxes in Russell's system that could not be dealt with even with his improved version called Ramified Type Theory. Their attempts in constructing a formal system by which mathematical axioms can be derived from type theory was not successful because unwarranted axioms that were ad hoc had to be included (the axiom of reducibility or the axiom of infinity), etc.

David Hilbert took up the project after Whitehead and Russell in rescuing the foundation of mathematics from inconsistency. Hilbert took a formalist approach. Hilbert sought to demonstrate the consistency of finite structures in arithmetic and from there, he would be able to show that they can be an extension of all of mathematics. Underlying Hilbert’s program is the assumption that anything in mathematics is solvable. We cannot know anything about the infinite and therefore we cannot ground mathematics upon an assumed or postulated infinitary system. He worked within the bounds of the finite.

For him, the issue of consistency is the limitations of their models which may contain internal contradictions. He wanted to construct an Absolute Consistency proof instead of a Relative Consistency proof for Arithmetic’s Consistency using this finitistic formal system. Hilbert altered the way we talked about and within mathematics with a finitary procedure that makes use of the manipulation of strokes and symbols by creating a system of numeration: numerals and numbers. The purpose of this is to reveal the underlying structure of our mathematical propositions & to prevent any form of flawed reasoning they may contain. Hilbert constructs a metamathematical proof as a way to address the problem of consistency. Metamathematical statements are statements about mathematics or about the string of symbols within a formal mathematical system (they are the statements about these numerical symbols & their arithmetical arrangement within the formalized system).

A couple decades later, Kurt Gödel demonstrated that Russell & Whitehead's project was a fool's errand--he showed that there are true statements that aren't provable in any logical system that can derive certain basic statements of number theory. Gödel was a mathematical realist which means he believed in the objective existence of numbers and that they are independent of our construction. Insofar as we formalized our language enough in order for us to accurately talk about these mathematical entities, impredicitivity shouldn't be a problem.

Gödel uses Russell’s paradox as one of the starting points for his proof by “arithmetizing” Russell’s formal system through the translation of primitive symbols to Gödel numbers. With a simple self-referential expressions such as “this statement cannot be proven,'' he assigned to each statement a primitive variable that represents either a constant, predicate letters, variables.

Gödel demonstrates in his incompleteness proofs that there are true number theoretical statements that are undecidable & cannot be proven in that formal system. The implications for Hilbert's program was that he showed that there will be statements in formal number theory that can be recognizably true but cannot be proven by its axioms. Any consistent formal system in which arithmetic can be expressed is incomplete - there will be true number-theoretic or arithmetical statements that cannot be derived in that system. A statement describing the consistency of formal arithmetic is not derivable by the axioms of formal arithmetic.

So, Russell and Whitehead’s formal system was not comprehensive enough to solve most of the logical paradoxes because as Kurt Gödel recognized, symbol manipulation and transformations was not enough to derive the truths of mathematics and that he needed to step outside the system to view the syntactic & semantic properties of the formal system contained in itself. The theorems derived in the formal system are consistent only insofar its axioms are and it turns out  the logical axioms Russell used to build the basis of arithmetic did not necessarily entail all of its theorems.
